## The result you will produce

```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
Your own branch
    → one checked Python change
    → two meaningful commits
    → one pull request for review
```

```bash
git status --short --branch
git log --oneline -2
```

::: {.key-idea}
Save a checked change, share it from your own branch, and show what changed.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 01:00–03:00 (2 minutes). Show the destination before teaching commands. The first
commit will add a baseline file; the second changes one income input. A pull
request proposes a change and provides a place to review it. It is not an
instruction for students to merge. Explain that outputs and commit hashes shown
in this lesson are examples; students will see their own values.
:::

## Git and GitHub have different jobs

::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}

### Git: on your computer

```bash
git status
git diff
git commit
```

Tracks versions and compares changes.

:::
::: {.column width="48%"}

### GitHub: in your browser

```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
Repository → Branch → Pull request
```

Hosts shared copies and review discussions.

:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 03:00–05:00 (2 minutes). Git is the version-control program; GitHub is the service we
use to share repositories and review proposed changes. Saving in an editor,
committing locally, and pushing to GitHub are three distinct actions. Do not
ask students to run the bare git commit example yet; the bounded command later
includes a message. The lines here name the operations we are about to learn.
:::

## Three local places, then the shared copy

```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
Working files  -- git add -->  Staged snapshot
                              |
                          git commit
                              v
                         Local history
                              |
                           git push
                              v
                         GitHub branch
```

**Saving a file** changes the working file. **Staging** chooses what the next commit records.

::: {.notes}
Clock 05:00–07:00 (2 minutes). A repository includes its Git history; the working files are
the version currently checked out. Staging records the selected content at the
time of git add. If a file changes again after staging, the later edits need
another git add to enter the next commit. A commit is a local snapshot with a
message; pushing shares commits. Avoid calling staging a permanent backup.
:::

## Use a terminal, not a Python code cell

In your prepared **terminal**:

```bash
git --version
```

::: {.terminal-output}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
git version 2.x.y
```
:::

- Keep the course Python environment available for running the script.
- Sign in to your GitHub account in the browser.
- Accept the instructor's collaborator invitation before the first push.

::: {.notes}
Clock 07:00–09:00 (2 minutes). The x and y are placeholders, not literal output to match.
These Git commands work in the prepared Windows, WSL, macOS or Linux terminal.
Keep all Git operations for this copy in the same environment. The Python
script is run using the already prepared course Python environment; Git itself
does not need pandas or another Python package. Handle authentication problems
with a helper rather than sharing an account or copying another student's token.
:::

## Get one working copy

If you do **not** already have a Git clone, run from its intended parent folder:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/swapnil1987/2026-research-methods.git
cd 2026-research-methods
```

If you already have a clone, open a terminal at its repository root instead.

::: {.small-note}
A downloaded ZIP contains files but no Git history. For this lesson, use a clone.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 09:00–12:00 (3 minutes). A clone includes the repository history and a configured
remote. Public cloning can work without collaborator permission; pushing later
requires authentication and permission. Do not clone inside an existing copy
or copy a .git folder by hand. Students with a standalone starter ZIP should
keep it and make a separate clone for the Git exercise. This does not require
deleting their earlier notebook work.
Reference: https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/cloning-a-repository
:::

## Check the repository and starting branch

From the **course repository root**:

```bash
git status --short --branch
git remote get-url origin
```

::: {.terminal-output}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
## main...origin/main
https://github.com/swapnil1987/2026-research-methods.git
```
:::

For an existing clone, preserve unexplained changes and ask for help.
Once the working tree is clean, update `main` before creating your branch:

```bash
git switch main
git pull --ff-only
```

::: {.notes}
Clock 12:00–15:00 (3 minutes). These are representative outputs from a clean clone on main.
Check both the directory and the branch; origin is the remote nickname created
by clone. If status lists existing changes, students should preserve them and
ask for help before switching branches or pulling. If they are on a previous
personal branch, only switch to main after confirming the working tree is
clean. Never use a reset or forced checkout to clear unexplained changes.
:::

## Set the identity recorded in commits

Replace both quoted placeholders with your own chosen details:

```bash
git config --local user.name "YOUR NAME"
git config --local user.email "YOUR COMMIT EMAIL"
git config --get user.name
git config --get user.email
```

Use your exact GitHub-provided **no-reply email** if you want to keep your usual email private.

::: {.small-note}
Commit identity is recorded in history. It does not sign you in to GitHub.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 15:00–17:00 (2 minutes). --local applies to this repository. Students should copy their
actual no-reply address from GitHub Settings > Emails rather than inventing one.
The name and email in public commits can be visible to others. Do not use the
private grade ID as the commit identity. GitHub authentication is a separate
step; changing user.name does not grant permission to push.
Reference: https://docs.github.com/en/account-and-profile/how-tos/email-preferences/setting-your-commit-email-address
:::

## Prepare authentication before pushing

```bash
git remote get-url origin
```

The course uses the **HTTPS** remote shown earlier.

1. Use the prepared Git credential setup, such as Git Credential Manager.
2. If it opens a browser, sign in with **your own account**.
3. If authentication fails, keep your local commits and ask for setup help.

::: {.key-idea}
Your GitHub account password is not a password for Git HTTPS operations.
Never put a token in a command, file, notebook, or screenshot.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 17:00–19:00 (2 minutes). Git Credential Manager can handle browser authentication and
secure credential storage when it is installed and configured. The exact
dialog depends on OS and credential setup. Do not promise that every Git
installation opens a browser automatically. GitHub no longer accepts account
passwords for Git HTTPS operations. The official guide also describes other
authentication methods; this lesson does not require installing gh CLI or
creating a token during class. References:
https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/git-basics/caching-your-github-credentials-in-git
https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/about-authentication-to-github
:::

Replace `YOUR-GITHUB-USERNAME` with your **public GitHub username** in every command.

```bash
git switch -c practice/YOUR-GITHUB-USERNAME
git branch --show-current
```

::: {.terminal-output}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
practice/YOUR-GITHUB-USERNAME
```
:::

::: {.key-idea}
Only the instructor can push or merge to `main`. Work on your own branch.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 19:00–21:00 (2 minutes). A branch names a line of commits; it is not a second folder.
All students begin from main but choose unique branch names. The displayed
username is a placeholder; their real output contains their public username.
Never put the privately assigned grade ID in branch names, files or PRs. If a
practice branch already exists, inspect it and use git switch with its name;
do not recreate it with a force option.
:::

## Check the baseline before recording it

Your new **`practice/YOUR-GITHUB-USERNAME/saving.py`** contains:

```python
income = 1000
consumption = 800
saving = income - consumption
print("Monthly saving (EUR):", saving)
```

In the **course Python terminal**, from the repository root:

```bash
python practice/YOUR-GITHUB-USERNAME/saving.py
```

::: {.answer .fragment}
Expected: `Monthly saving (EUR): 200`. Verify `1000 - 800` by hand.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 24:00–26:00 (2 minutes). Saving is EUR per month for one synthetic household. The
script needs no dataset or external package. Students must save the new file
before running it, and the terminal must use the prepared Python environment.
If the path fails, first check the repository root and the actual username
folder. Do not change the shared starter script.
:::

## `status` shows what Git has noticed

```bash
git status --short
```

::: {.terminal-output}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
?? practice/
```
:::

`??` means **untracked**: the new file has not been staged or committed.

::: {.small-note}
Git may show the whole new folder first. Inspect the exact file you intend to add.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 26:00–28:00 (2 minutes). In a fresh clone, practice may not exist before this exercise,
so short status commonly groups untracked files under practice/. If that
directory already contains tracked work, Git may show a more specific path.
Do not require exact equality with this illustrative output. status reports
state; it does not record a version or send anything to GitHub.
:::

## Stage the exact file, then inspect it

```bash
git add -- practice/YOUR-GITHUB-USERNAME/saving.py
git diff --cached -- practice/YOUR-GITHUB-USERNAME/saving.py
git status --short
```

::: {.terminal-output}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
A  practice/YOUR-GITHUB-USERNAME/saving.py
```
:::

`A` in the first column means **staged addition**. `--cached` shows the staged content.

::: {.notes}
Clock 28:00–30:00 (2 minutes). Inspect the staged diff before committing. git add takes a
snapshot of this file's current content. Later edits are not automatically
staged. -- separates options from the path. Avoid git add . in this shared
course exercise: an unrelated notebook, generated output or credential should
not be accidentally included. The actual diff will include headers and + lines.
Reference: https://git-scm.com/docs/git-add
:::

## Commit a checked baseline

```bash
git commit -m "Add baseline household saving calculation"
git status --short
git log --oneline -1
```

::: {.terminal-output}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
a1b2c3d Add baseline household saving calculation
```
:::

The hash above is illustrative. Your own short hash will differ.

::: {.key-idea}
A commit records the staged snapshot locally. It has not been pushed yet.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 30:00–32:00 (2 minutes). The real commit command also prints a summary, omitted here;
the example shown is the output of git log. A clean git status --short prints
no changed paths. If other files are listed, preserve and inspect them rather
than trying to make the screen match by deleting them. Prefer a message that
describes the change over a message such as update or final.
:::

## Watch first · Make one small change

In the instructor's own **practice file**, change only the income input:

```diff
-income = 1000
+income = 1200
```

Save, then run the script:

```bash
python practice/YOUR-GITHUB-USERNAME/saving.py
```

::: {.answer .fragment}
Expected: `Monthly saving (EUR): 400`.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 32:00–35:00 (3 minutes). This is a short instructor demonstration; students repeat
the change in the upcoming exercise. Say explicitly which file is being
edited. Saving in the editor changes the working file, not the previous
commit. Both input cases are synthetic, positive-income examples. Recheck
1200 - 800 by hand before trusting the output.
:::

## Inspect the change with `diff`

```bash
git diff -- practice/YOUR-GITHUB-USERNAME/saving.py
```

The relevant lines of the diff are:

```diff
-income = 1000
+income = 1200
```

- `-` is the old line; `+` is the new line.
- Here, plain `git diff` compares unstaged edits with the staged snapshot.

::: {.notes}
Clock 35:00–38:00 (3 minutes). With no currently staged changes, the staged snapshot still
matches the baseline commit. The actual output includes paths, hashes, @@
location information and unchanged context lines; focus attention on the two
changed lines. The leading +/- symbols are diff notation, not characters to
type into Python. After git add, plain git diff can be empty even though a
change is staged; use git diff --cached for that comparison.
:::

## Your turn · Save, run, and review

::: {.exercise}
1. In your own `saving.py`, change income from `1000` to `1200` and save.
2. Predict the saving, then run the script and check the result.
3. Run the two commands below. Explain which line changed and whether it is staged.
:::

```bash
git diff -- practice/YOUR-GITHUB-USERNAME/saving.py
git status --short
```

::: {.answer .fragment}
Saving is `400`. Before staging, status shows a modification in its second column: ` M`.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 38:00–43:00 (5 minutes). Allocate three minutes to the individual change and checks,
then two to explanations in pairs. Students should be editing their own
personal file, not codes/lecture-5/saving_start.py. If the script still prints
200, check that the editor saved and that Python ran the same file. Ask what
an empty diff means only after establishing whether the change was staged.
:::

## Record the change you just checked

```bash
git add -- practice/YOUR-GITHUB-USERNAME/saving.py
git diff --cached -- practice/YOUR-GITHUB-USERNAME/saving.py
git commit -m "Check saving with income of 1200 EUR"
git status --short
```

::: {.key-idea}
Inspect the staged diff again. Record one understandable change per commit.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 43:00–45:00 (2 minutes). Students should review that only the income line changed.
The commit message records the calculation being checked rather than merely
saying the file was saved. If the file was edited after staging, repeat git
add for that specific path and recheck the staged diff. No force operations
are needed, and nothing should be committed on main in this workflow.
:::

## Read your local history

```bash
git log --oneline -2
git show --stat --oneline HEAD
```

::: {.terminal-output}
```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
d4e5f6a Check saving with income of 1200 EUR
a1b2c3d Add baseline household saving calculation
```
:::

Newest first. **`HEAD`** identifies the currently checked-out commit.

::: {.notes}
Clock 45:00–47:00 (2 minutes). The displayed hashes are illustrative. git show --stat adds
a compact summary of files changed in the newest commit; that extra output is
not shown in this abbreviated example. A meaningful sequence helps a reviewer
understand the baseline and the change. A commit is not proof that the
calculation is correct; retain the hand check and executable result.
:::

## Push your own branch to GitHub

First confirm the branch, then push it:

```bash
git branch --show-current
git push -u origin practice/YOUR-GITHUB-USERNAME
git status --short --branch
```

`-u` records the upstream for this local branch. On later pushes from it, use `git push`.

::: {.small-note}
Push only your own practice branch. If authentication or permission fails,
your local commits are still saved.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 47:00–50:00 (3 minutes). The first push creates the corresponding branch on origin
if it does not exist and the account has permission. The instructor must have
invited the student's account as a collaborator and the student must have
accepted. Never solve a rejection by pushing to main, forcing a push or using
someone else's credentials. If the branch already exists remotely with
unexpected history, stop and inspect with help.
:::

## Open a pull request in the browser

On the course repository's **GitHub page**:

```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
Pull requests → New pull request
base: main
compare: practice/YOUR-GITHUB-USERNAME
```

1. Check **Files changed** contains only your practice file.
2. Give the PR a clear title and describe the change and your check.
3. Choose **Create pull request**, then leave it for the instructor to review.

::: {.notes}
Clock 50:00–53:00 (3 minutes). GitHub may also offer Compare & pull request after a push.
The essential choice is base main and compare the student's own branch; do
not reverse them. Explain that opening a PR does not merge it. This is
classroom practice, not the graded Exercise 1 submission. The later task sheet
will state assignment paths, deadline and rubric. Reference:
https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/how-tos/create-pull-requests/creating-a-pull-request
:::

## A useful PR describes evidence

```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
Title: Check saving after a higher income input

Changed income from 1000 to 1200 EUR per month.
Consumption stays at 800 EUR per month.
Hand check: 1200 - 800 = 400.
Ran saving.py; it prints Monthly saving (EUR): 400.
```

For a requested correction, edit your file on the **same branch**, check it,
commit it, and run `git push`. The open PR then includes the new commit.

::: {.notes}
Clock 53:00–55:00 (2 minutes). Keep the explanation short and concrete. Students should not
include private grade IDs, credentials or confidential data in a public PR.
The instructor reviews and decides whether to merge; only the instructor may
update main. For graded submissions, later commits do not retroactively change
the version captured at the deadline under the syllabus policy.
:::

## Keep source inputs separate from outputs

The repository's `.gitignore` includes patterns such as:

```{.text code-line-numbers="false"}
__pycache__/
.ipynb_checkpoints/
codes/**/outputs/*
!codes/**/outputs/README.md
```

```bash
git status --short
git diff --cached --name-only
```

Commit the intended source and instructions. Inspect generated files before including them.

::: {.notes}
Clock 55:00–57:00 (2 minutes). The script in this lesson prints output, so it does not create
an output file. The shown patterns already exist in the course .gitignore;
students need not edit that shared file. Supplied synthetic raw data can be
versioned; never overwrite it casually. .gitignore helps exclude untracked
files, but does not remove files already tracked. No ignore pattern replaces
checking the staged file list. Do not say that all CSVs should be ignored.
:::

## If something looks wrong, inspect before changing it

```bash
git status --short --branch
git remote get-url origin
git diff
git diff --cached
```

- Wrong folder? Return to the intended clone.
- Unexpected changes or a rejected push? Preserve the work and ask for help.
- Leave other students' branches and the protected `main` branch alone.

::: {.notes}
Clock 57:00–58:00 (1 minute). The hour does not teach destructive recovery commands,
rebasing, conflict resolution or force pushes. Reassure students that a failed
push does not erase their local commits. A helper should inspect actual status
and the error message before proposing a fix. Do not run cleanup commands on
the course checkout just to demonstrate failure recovery.
:::

## Exit check · Which action does what?

```bash
git add -- practice/YOUR-GITHUB-USERNAME/saving.py
git commit -m "Describe the checked change"
git push
```

Before running anything, identify the action that **stages**, **records locally**,
and **shares commits**. Who may merge your PR into `main`?

::: {.answer .fragment}
`add` stages; `commit` records locally; `push` shares. Only the instructor may merge to `main`.
:::

::: {.notes}
Clock 58:00–60:00 (2 minutes). This is an explanation question, not an instruction to make
an empty extra commit. Confirm each student can show the intended branch and
PR link, or explain the specific unresolved setup problem. References and
step-by-step commands are in codes/lecture-5/README.md. Course workflow is a
collaborator workflow; forking is a different option, not required here.
:::
